name: Clear Linux or Mac System Logs
description:
Adversaries may clear system logs to hide evidence of an intrusion. macOS and Linux both keep track of system or user-initiated actions via system logs. The majority of native system logging is stored under the `/var/log/` directory. Subfolders in this directory categorize logs by their related functions, such as:(Citation: Linux Logs)

* `/var/log/messages:`: General and system-related messages
* `/var/log/secure or /var/log/auth.log`: Authentication logs
* `/var/log/utmp or /var/log/wtmp`: Login records
* `/var/log/kern.log`: Kernel logs
* `/var/log/cron.log`: Crond logs
* `/var/log/maillog`: Mail server logs
* `/var/log/httpd/`: Web server access and error logs

references.description: Marcel. (2018, April 19). 12 Critical Linux Log Files You Must be Monitoring. Retrieved March 29, 2020.

telemetry.collection_focus: Prefer Sysmon FileDeleteDetected (26) when content retention is not needed; FileDelete (23) also archives files and requires a storage/privacy plan.

configuration: On a disposable Windows host, review the installed Sysmon schema and current configuration; merge scoped event filters into the existing policy rather than replacing it.
Forward Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational to the lab collector. Preserve event ID, timestamp, computer, process identifiers and the original event.
For Linux or macOS, select the equivalent sensor separately and test its emitted fields; a Windows event ID does not transfer across platforms.
telemetry.example_note: Project-normalized synthetic JSON, not a native provider log, captured event, attack verdict or validated detection. A parser/adapter is required for a real SIEM. Example names, IPs and values are fictional.
telemetry.limitations: Event filtering and sensor versions change coverage. High-volume image-load and process-access collection needs tuning; endpoint events alone do not establish intent.

sigma_rules.title: Clear or Disable Kernel Ring Buffer Logs via Syslog Syscall

logsource.definition:
Required auditd configuration:
-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S syslog -F a0=4 -k clear_dmesg_logs
-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S syslog -F a0=5 -k clear_dmesg_logs
-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S syslog -F a0=6 -k disable_dmesg_logs
-a always,exit -F arch=b32 -S syslog -F a0=4 -k clear_dmesg_logs
-a always,exit -F arch=b32 -S syslog -F a0=5 -k clear_dmesg_logs
-a always,exit -F arch=b32 -S syslog -F a0=6 -k disable_dmesg_logs

strategies.name: Behavioral Detection of Log File Clearing on Linux and macOS

analytics.name: Analytic 1438
analytics.guidance: Detects log-clearing behavior by correlating suspicious command execution targeting log files under /var/log/, anomalous deletions or truncations of system logs, and unusual child processes (e.g., shell pipelines or redirections).

tuning.description: The time window used to correlate log file interaction and suspicious command execution.
Regex pattern used to match monitored log file paths (e.g., /var/log/auth.log).
User or group (e.g., root) that should trigger higher severity detection.

analytics.name: Analytic 1439
analytics.guidance: Detects adversary clearing log files on macOS by correlating calls to shell utilities (e.g., echo >, rm, truncate) targeting files in /var/log/ with unusual context (non-administrative users or abnormal process lineage).

tuning.description: Duration in which process activity and file I/O should be temporally linked.
Tunable path filter for macOS logs such as /var/log/system.log or /var/log/asl.log.
Detects higher risk when log deletion is performed by unusual users (e.g., interactive vs. system users).

software.name: Proton
software.description: [Proton](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0279) removes logs from /var/logs and /Library/logs.(Citation: objsee mac malware 2017)

references.description: Patrick Wardle. (n.d.). Mac Malware of 2017. Retrieved September 21, 2018.

software.name: MacMa
software.description: [MacMa](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1016) can clear possible malware traces such as application logs.(Citation: ESET DazzleSpy Jan 2022)

references.description: M.Léveillé, M., Cherepanov, A.. (2022, January 25). Watering hole deploys new macOS malware, DazzleSpy, in Asia. Retrieved May 6, 2022.

software.name: UPSTYLE
software.description: [UPSTYLE](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1164) clears error logs after reading embedded commands for execution.(Citation: Volexity UPSTYLE 2024)

references.description: Volexity Threat Research. (2024, April 12). Zero-Day Exploitation of Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution Vulnerability in GlobalProtect (CVE-2024-3400). Retrieved November 20, 2024.

software.name: JumbledPath
software.description: [JumbledPath](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1206) can clear logs on all devices used along its connection path to compromised network infrastructure.(Citation: Cisco Salt Typhoon FEB 2025)

references.description: Cisco Talos. (2025, February 20). Weathering the storm: In the midst of a Typhoon. Retrieved February 24, 2025.

actors.name: Rocke
actors.description: [Rocke](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0106) has cleared log files within the /var/log/ folder.(Citation: Anomali Rocke March 2019)

references.description: Anomali Labs. (2019, March 15). Rocke Evolves Its Arsenal With a New Malware Family Written in Golang. Retrieved April 24, 2019.

actors.name: TeamTNT
actors.description: [TeamTNT](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0139) has removed system logs from /var/log/syslog.(Citation: Aqua TeamTNT August 2020)

references.description: Kol, Roi. Morag, A. (2020, August 25). Deep Analysis of TeamTNT Techniques Using Container Images to Attack. Retrieved September 22, 2021.

actors.name: Sea Turtle
actors.description: [Sea Turtle](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1041) has overwritten Linux system logs and unsets the Bash history file (effectively removing logging) during intrusions.(Citation: Hunt Sea Turtle 2024)

references.description: Hunt & Hackett Research Team. (2024, January 5). Turkish espionage campaigns in the Netherlands. Retrieved November 20, 2024.

actors.name: Salt Typhoon
actors.description: [Salt Typhoon](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1045) has cleared logs including .bash_history, auth.log, lastlog, wtmp, and btmp.(Citation: Cisco Salt Typhoon FEB 2025)

references.description: Cisco Talos. (2025, February 20). Weathering the storm: In the midst of a Typhoon. Retrieved February 24, 2025.

mitigations.name: Restrict File and Directory Permissions
mitigations.description: Protect generated event files that are stored locally with proper permissions and authentication and limit opportunities for adversaries to increase privileges by preventing Privilege Escalation opportunities.

mitigations.name: Remote Data Storage
mitigations.description: Automatically forward events to a log server or data repository to prevent conditions in which the adversary can locate and manipulate data on the local system. When possible, minimize time delay on event reporting to avoid prolonged storage on the local system.

mitigations.name: Encrypt Sensitive Information
mitigations.description: Obfuscate/encrypt event files locally and in transit to avoid giving feedback to an adversary.

candidates.name: Overwrite macOS system log via echo utility
candidates.description: This test overwrites the contents of system log file with an empty string using echo utility

candidates.name: Delete system log files via unlink utility
candidates.description: This test deletes the system log file using unlink utility

candidates.name: Overwrite FreeBSD system log via echo utility
candidates.description: This test overwrites the contents of system log file with an empty string using echo utility

candidates.name: Truncate system log files via truncate utility (freebsd)
candidates.description: This test truncates the system log files using the truncate utility with (-s 0 or --size=0) parameter which sets file size to zero, thus emptying the file content

candidates.name: Overwrite Linux Mail Spool
candidates.description: This test overwrites the Linux mail spool of a specified user. This technique was used by threat actor Rocke during the exploitation of Linux web servers.

candidates.name: Delete log files via cat utility by appending /dev/null or /dev/zero (freebsd)
candidates.description: The first sub-test truncates the log file to zero bytes via /dev/null and the second sub-test fills the log file with null bytes(zeroes) via /dev/zero, using cat utility

candidates.name: Delete system log files via unlink utility (freebsd)
candidates.description: This test deletes the messages log file using unlink utility

candidates.name: Truncate system log files via truncate utility
candidates.description: This test truncates the system log files using the truncate utility with (-s 0) parameter which sets file size to zero, thus emptying the file content

system_log_path.description: path of system log to delete.

candidates.name: Delete log files using built-in log utility
candidates.description: This test deletes main log datastore, inflight log data, time-to-live data(TTL), fault and error content

candidates.name: Delete system log files using OSAScript
candidates.description: This test deletes the system log file using osascript via "do shell script"(sh/bash by default) which in-turn spawns rm utility, requires admin privileges

candidates.name: Real-time system log clearance/deletion
candidates.description: This test reads real-time system log file and writes empty string to it, thus clearing the log file without tampering with the logging process

candidates.name: Delete system log files using shred utility
candidates.description: This test overwrites the contents of the log file with zero bytes(-z) using three passes(-n 3) of data, and then delete the file(-u) securely

candidates.name: rm -rf
candidates.description: Delete system and audit logs

syslog_path.description: path of syslog file to delete. On macos it's /var/log/system.log*, on linux, it's /var/log/syslog*. Also note for File events, that on macos, /var/ is a link to /private/var/.

macos_audit_path.description: path of audit file to delete

candidates.name: Delete system log files using srm utility
candidates.description:
This test securely deletes the system log files individually and recursively using the srm utility.
Install srm using Homebrew with the command: brew install khell/homebrew-srm/srm
Refer: https://github.com/khell/homebrew-srm/issues/1 for installation

candidates.name: System log file deletion via find utility
candidates.description: This test finds and deletes the system log files within /var/log/ directory using various executions(rm, shred, unlink)

system_log_name1.description: name or prefix of system log to delete.

system_log_name2.description: name or prefix of system log to delete.

system_log_name3.description: name or prefix of system log to delete.

candidates.name: rm -rf
candidates.description: Delete messages and security logs

candidates.name: Delete log files via cat utility by appending /dev/null or /dev/zero
candidates.description: The first sub-test truncates the log file to zero bytes via /dev/null and the second sub-test fills the log file with null bytes(zeroes) via /dev/zero, using cat utility

system_log_path.description: path of system log to delete.

candidates.name: Delete system journal logs via rm and journalctl utilities
candidates.description: The first sub-test deletes the journal files using rm utility in the "/var/log/journal/" directory and the second sub-test clears the journal by modifiying time period of logs that should be retained to zero.

candidates.name: Overwrite Linux Log
candidates.description: This test overwrites the specified log. This technique was used by threat actor Rocke during the exploitation of Linux web servers.

candidates.name: Delete system log files using Applescript
candidates.description:
This test deletes the system log file using applescript using osascript via Finder application
Note: The user may be prompted to grant access to the Finder application before the command can be executed successfully as part of TCC(Transparency, Consent, and Control) Framework.
Refer: https://www.rainforestqa.com/blog/macos-tcc-db-deep-dive
